title: Revisiting Degree-Corrected Spectral Clustering: a Condition-Free Spectral Analysis and Extension

paper.title: Revisiting Degree-Corrected Spectral Clustering: a Condition-Free Spectral Analysis and Extension
paper.abstract: Abstract Spectral clustering is a representative graph clustering technique with strong interpretability and theoretical guarantees. Degree-corrected spectral clustering (DCSC) has emerged as the state-of-the-art for this technique. While prior studies have provided impressive theoretical insights for DCSC, their analyses typically depend on specific probabilistic frameworks (e.g., stochastic block models) and conditions. In this study, we explore an alternative condition-free analysis for the clustering quality of DCSC from a pure spectral view, without any random graph models. It gives bounds for the number of mis-clustered nodes w.r.t. the optimal partition of conductance minimization while involving quantities that indicate impacts of (i) degree heterogeneity and (ii) weakness of clustering structures to the clustering quality. Inspired by graph neural networks (GNNs) and their over-smoothing effect, we propose ASCENT (Adaptive Spectral ClustEring with Node-wise correcTion), a simple yet effective extension of DCSC. Different from most DCSC methods with a constant degree correction, ASCENT follows a node-wise correction scheme. It can assign different corrections for nodes via a GNN mean aggregator. We demonstrate that (i) ASCENT reduces to conventional DCSC methods when encountering over-smoothing; (ii) some early stages before over-smoothing can potentially result in better clustering quality.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Graph clustering (a.k.a. disjoint community detection) is a classic inference task that partitions nodes of a graph into densely connected groups (i.e., clusters or communities). Since the extracted clusters have been validated to correspond to some substructures of real-world systems (e.g., functional groups in protein interactions [ 1 ] ), many network applications are formulated as graph clustering, including protein complex detection [ 2 ] , cellular network decomposition [ 3 ] , and Internet traffic profiling [ 4 ] . Spectral clustering (SC) is one of the representative techniques for this task. In the past few decades, a series of SC methods have been proposed. Ding et al. [ 18 ] provided an overview of related research. Table 2 summarizes some representative theoretical results about the clustering quality of DCSC. For instance, Chaudhuri et al. [ 12 ] proposed a DCSC method for graphs drawn from an extended planted partition (EPP) model [ 19 ] and examined its quality guarantees w.r.t. the optimal separation of EPP. Qin and Rohe [ 7 ] analyzed the quality bound of RSC in terms of mis-clustered rate using the degree-corrected stochastic blockmodel (DCSBM) [ 20 ] and provided guidance on the choice of τ \tau . Also based on DCSBM, Qing et al. [ 9 ] and Jin et al [ 8 ] respectively proposed ISC and SCORE+ , which have theoretical guarantees about the Hamming error rate w.r.t. ground-truth. Cohen-Addad et al. [ 17 ] introduced the degree-heterogeneous stochastic blockmodel (DHSBM) and proved that there exists a linear-time spectral algorithm with bounded recovery probability for DHSBM. In summary, most related theoretical studies rely on assumptions of random graph models (e.g., DCSBM). They usually fit the adjacency matrix or graph Laplacian using a certain random graph model (e.g., 𝒜 := 𝚯 ​ 𝐙𝐁𝐙 T ​ 𝚯 \mathcal{A}:={\bf{\Theta ZB}}{{\bf{Z}}^{T}}{\bf{\Theta}} [ 7 , 9 ] with { 𝚯 , 𝐙 , 𝐁 } \{{\bf{\Theta}},{\bf{Z}},{\bf{B}}\} defined in DCSBM) and give bounds related to such a model (e.g., mis-clustered rate or error w.r.t. the ground-truth of DCSBM in Table 2 ). Moreover, most of them presuppose some additional conditions or assumptions (e.g., [ K ​ ln ⁡ ( 4 ​ N / ϵ ) / ( d ¯ min + τ ) ] 1 / 2 ≤ λ K / ( 8 ​ 3 ) [K\ln(4N/\epsilon)/(\bar{d}_{\min}+\tau)]^{1/2}\leq{\lambda_{K}}/(8\sqrt{3}) and d ¯ min + τ > 3 ​ ln ⁡ ( 4 ​ N / ε ) {\bar{d}_{\min}}+\tau>3\ln(4N/\varepsilon) for RSC in [ 7 ] ; [ ln ⁡ ( 4 ​ N / ε ) / ( d ¯ min + τ ) ] 1 / 2 ≤ λ K / 8 ​ 3 {[\ln(4N/\varepsilon)/({{\bar{d}}_{\min}}+\tau)]^{1/2}}\leq{\lambda_{K}}/8\sqrt{3} and d ¯ min + τ > 3 ​ ln ⁡ ( 4 ​ N / ε ) {{\bar{d}}_{\min}}+\tau>3\ln(4N/\varepsilon) for ISC in [ 9 ] ), which may fail in some extreme cases (e.g., for a large number of nodes N N ) and thus result in trivial theoretical results. Present Analysis & Extension . SC is a typical approximated algorithm for the NP-hard combinatorial optimization of graph-cut minimization [ 21 ] . From this perspective, some prior work [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] analyzed vanilla SC (e.g., NJW ) using the spectral graph theory. Motivated by these studies, we consider an alternative condition-free analysis for the clustering quality of DCSC from a pure spectral view instead of using any random graph models . Different from existing analyses with bounds related to random graph models (e.g., DCSBM in Table 2 ), we provide bounds for the number of mis-clustered nodes w.r.t. the optimal solution to average conductance minimization. In contrast to early spectral-based studies on vanilla SC [ 22 , 23 ] , our analysis also involves quantities about (i) degree heterogeneity and (ii) weakness of clustering structures, which can reveal impacts of these two aspects to the clustering quality of DCSC. Inspired by graph neural networks (GNNs), we propose ASCENT ( A daptive S pectral C lust E ring with N ode-wise correc T ion), a simple yet effective extension of DCSC. Instead of using a constant correction τ \tau for all nodes (e.g., RSC , SCORE+ , and ISC in Table 1 ), ASCENT adopts a node-wise correction scheme, where nodes { v i } \{v_{i}\} can be assigned with different corrections { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} . This scheme iteratively updates { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} via a GNN mean aggregator, where nodes { v i } \{v_{i}\} with more common neighbors (e.g., in the same cluster) are more likely to have closer { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} . Consistent with the over-smoothing effect of GNNs, { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} finally converge to a constant. In this case, ASCENT reduces to conventional DCSC methods. Our experiments demonstrate that some early stages of this updating procedure (i.e., before over-smoothing) can potentially result in better clustering quality. We also extend our analysis to a unified framework that provides bounds for a series of SC methods. Based on this framework, we try to answer the following three questions. • Q1 : Can DCSC achieve a tighter bound than vanilla SC? • Q2 : Can ISC achieve a tighter bound than RSC ? • Q3 : Can ASCENT achieve a tighter bound than ISC ? Answering Q1 - Q3 may help interpret why a DCSC method outperforms others. Whereas, most related studies tend to focus on a single algorithm and may not be able to answer these questions explored in this paper. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work. Formal problem statements and preliminaries of this study are given in Section 3 . Section 4 presents our condition-free spectral analysis for the clustering quality of DCSC, while Section 5 elaborates on the extended ASCENT algorithm. Empirical experiments are further described in Section 6 . Finally, Section 7 concludes this paper and discusses possible future research directions to tackle limitations of this study.

sections.heading: 2.1 Theoretical Analyses of (Degree-Corrected) Spectral Clustering
sections.text: In addition to the theoretical analyses on clustering quality shown in Table 2 , there are studies focusing on other aspects about (DC)SC as summarized in Table 3 . For instance, Lee et al. [ 25 ] provided a theoretical justification of using leading K K eigenvectors [ 𝐮 1 , ⋯ , 𝐮 K ] [{\bf{u}}_{1},\cdots,{\bf{u}}_{K}] for SC and investigated associated properties about graph topology. Based on the detectability analyses on DCSBM [ 31 , 32 ] , several studies try to reveal inherent spectrum properties (e.g., distribution of leading eigenvalues) of the non-backtracking matrix [ 26 , 27 ] and Bethe-Hessian matrix [ 28 , 29 , 30 ] , which were further used to design new (DC)SC algorithms. While we acknowledge prior studies summarized in Table 3, which explore spectral properties of specific matrices or detectability under certain random graph models, we note that their focus differs from the main objective of this work (i.e., the analysis of quality bounds for DCSC). Consequently, a direct quantitative comparison between these prior results and our theoretical bounds may not be readily feasible. Furthermore, most of them still rely on specific conditions and random graph models (e.g., DCSBM). In contrast, our analysis offers a distinct perspective by providing a condition-free bound derived purely from spectral theory, without recourse to any underlying random graph model.

sections.heading: 2.2 Applications of Deep Graph Clustering
sections.text: In recent years, several deep graph clustering (DGC) methods have been proposed as reviewed by Liu et al. [ 33 ] and Su et al. [ 34 ] . GraphEncoder [ 35 ] and DNR [ 36 ] are early studies that learn low-dimensional community-preserving representations (or embeddings) by reconstructing topology-related features (e.g., normalized adjacency matrices and modularity matrices) via a deep auto-encoder. THESAURUS [ 37 ] enhances the ability of learned embeddings to capture implicit graph clustering structures by using (i) context-aware semantic prototypes, (ii) a cross-view assignment prediction objective, and (iii) Gromov-Wasserstein Optimal Transport. For clustering on large-scale graphs, Devvrit et al. [ 38 ] proposed S3GC , which learns scalable community-preserving embeddings via GNN-based contrastive learning. MAGI [ 39 ] extends S3GC to incorporate the modularity maximization objective [ 40 ] from the view of contrastive learning. A downstream clustering algorithm (e.g., K K Means) is usually applied to the learned embeddings to derive a feasible clustering result for these approaches. DGCluster [ 41 ] also uses the modularity maximization objective to optimize GNN, which outputs community-preserving embeddings, but derives final clustering results using BIRCH [ 42 ] . ClusterNet [ 43 ] , MinCutPool [ 44 ] , and DMoN [ 45 ] adopt a deep end-to-end structure, which contains a GNN and an output module (e.g., a multi-layer perceptron for deriving clustering results), to fit classic graph clustering objectives (e.g., graph-cut minimization and modularity maximization). SDCN [ 46 ] combines the deep auto-encoder with GNN and uses a dual self-supervised mechanism to unify these two deep architectures. Most of the aforementioned methods, especially those based on GNNs, were originally designed for attributed graphs and may not fully consider the complicated correlations between graph topology and attributes (see Section 3 for further discussions). Our empirical experiments (see Section 6 ) demonstrated that when attributes are unavailable, these state-of-the-art DGC methods may not outperform SC approaches. Different from SC, most related studies about DGC may also lack interpretability and theoretical guarantees.

4 Proposed Analysis on Clustering Quality of DCSC: A Spectral View
sections.text: Inspired by prior spectral-based studies on vanilla SC [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] , we propose a condition-free analysis for the clustering quality of DCSC from a pure spectral view instead of using random graph models. We adopt ISC (see Table 1 ) as an example for analysis because it has a more generic format involving the reweighted ( K + 1 ) (K+1) leading eigenvectors [ λ 1 ​ 𝐮 1 , ⋯ , λ K + 1 ​ 𝐮 K + 1 ] [{\lambda_{1}}{{\bf{u}}_{1}},\cdots,{\lambda_{K+1}}{{\bf{u}}_{K+1}}] . Whereas, other DCSC methods have simpler formats (e.g., only [ 𝐮 1 , ⋯ , 𝐮 K ] [{\bf{u}}_{1},\cdots,{\bf{u}}_{K}] for RSC ). We then reduce this analysis to other algorithms (e.g., NJW , SCORE+ , and RSC ), which form a unified framework with theoretical bounds for a series of (DC)SC approaches.

sections.heading: 5 Extension of DCSC: ASCENT
sections.text: Inspired by recent advances in GNNs, we introduce ASCENT, a simple yet effective extension of DCSC. Different from most DCSC methods with a constant correction τ \tau (e.g., RSC , SCORE+ , and ISC in Table 1 ), ASCENT adopts a node-wise correction scheme. It can determine different corrections { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} for nodes { v i } \{v_{i}\} via an iterative aggregation mechanism that computes ‘local’ average degrees w.r.t. graph topology. Whereas, τ \tau is usually set to be a ‘global’ average degree for existing DCSC algorithms (e.g., τ = d ¯ \tau=\bar{d} for RSC ).

sections.heading: 5.3 Complexity Analysis
sections.text: Given a large-scale graph, we usually have K , L ≪ N < | E | K,L\ll N<|E| . Assume that the graph to be partitioned is sparse. For ASCENT, the time complexity of deriving node-wise corrections { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} is no more than O ⁡ ( | E | ​ L ) = O ⁡ ( | E | ) O(|E|L)=O(|E|) by fully utilizing the sparsity of a graph and sparse-dense matrix multiplication operation. ASCENT follows the same steps of (i) ED, (ii) spectral embedding arrangement, (iii) embedding normalization, and (iv) K K Means clustering with ISC , which have complexities of (i) O ⁡ ( ( N + | E | ) ​ K ) = O ⁡ ( N + | E | ) O((N+|E|)K)=O(N+|E|) (e.g., via the efficient Lanczos algorithm [ 56 ] for ED), (ii) O ⁡ ( N ​ K ) = O ⁡ ( N ) O(NK)=O(N) , (iii) O ⁡ ( N ​ K ) = O ⁡ ( N ) O(NK)=O(N) , and (iv) O ⁡ ( N ​ K 2 ​ t ) = O ⁡ ( N ) O(NK^{2}t)=O(N) (with t ≪ N t\ll N as the number of iterations in K K Means), respectively. In summary, the overall time complexity of ASCENT is about O ⁡ ( N + | E | ) O(N+|E|) . It has the same complexity as most existing DCSC algorithms. Therefore, the additional step of deriving node-wise corrections { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} will not increase the complexity of ASCENT .

sections.heading: 6.1 Experiment Setup
sections.text: Datasets . We used 2 2 settings of synthetic benchmarks and 12 12 real graphs for evaluation. Table 5 summarizes their statistics, where N N , | E | |E| , and K K are the numbers of nodes, edges, and clusters (if available); d d denotes node degree. In particular, these datasets cover various scales, with N N increasing from about 500 500 to more than 3 × 10 6 3\times 10^{6} , which can effectively test the scalability of a graph clustering method. LFR-net [ 57 ] is a synthetic benchmark that simulates properties of real-world graphs. It uses ( d ¯ , d max , c min , c max , η ) ({\bar{d}},{d_{\max}},{c_{\min}},{c_{\max}},\eta) to generate a graph, where d ¯ {\bar{d}} and d max {d_{\max}} are the average and maximum degrees; c min {c_{\min}} and c max {c_{\max}} are the minimum and maximum cluster sizes; η \eta is the ratio between the external degree and total degree of a node v i v_{i} w.r.t. the cluster v i v_{i} belongs to. To test the ability to handle (i) weak clustering structures and (ii) high degree heterogeneity, we generated two sets of graphs, denoted as LFR-1 and LFR-2 . For LFR-1 , we fixed ( N , d ¯ , d max , c min , c max ) = ( 2000 , 50 , 1000 , 50 , 500 ) (N,{\bar{d}},d_{\max},c_{\min},c_{\max})=(2000,50,1000,50,500) and adjusted η ∈ { 0.1 , 0.3 , 0.5 } \eta\in\{0.1,0.3,0.5\} . With the increase of η \eta , clustering structures become weaker . For LFR-2 , we fixed ( N , d max , c min , c max , η ) = ( 2000 , 1000 , 50 , 500 , 0.5 ) (N,d_{\max},c_{\min},c_{\max},\eta)=(2000,1000,50,500,0.5) and set d ¯ ∈ { 10 , 20 , 30 } {\bar{d}}\in\{10,20,30\} , where lower d ¯ \bar{d} implies higher degree heterogeneity . Caltech [ 58 ] and Simmons [ 58 ] are two graphs regarding friendships of two online social networks. PolBlogs [ 59 ] is a graph constructed based on the links between blogs with different political leanings. Wiki [ 60 ] is a co-occurrence graph of words that appear in the first million bytes of the Wikipedia dump. BlogCatalog [ 60 ] was extracted from social relationships provided by blogger authors. PPI [ 60 ] , BioGrid [ 61 ] , and ogbn-Protein [ 62 ] are three protein-protein interaction graphs. LiveJournal [ 63 ] and Orkut [ 63 ] were constructed based on the friendship relations in the online social networks of LiveJournal and Orkut. RoadCA [ 64 ] describes intersections and endpoints of a road network in California. ogbn-Products [ 65 ] is a graph representing an Amazon product co-purchasing network. During preprocessing, we followed [ 2 ] to extract the clustering ground-truth of BioGrid , where the complex set CYC2008 [ 66 ] with 231 231 protein complexes was used as the reference set. For the rest datasets, we used their original formats. Note that we could not use ground-truth of PPI , Wiki , BlogCatalog , LiveJournal , and Orkut , which describe overlapping community structures, as we consider disjoint graph partitioning. As stated in Section 3 , we assume that graph attributes are unavailable. ogbn-Protein and ogbn-Products are attributed graphs for the evaluation of node classification. We did not use their ground-truth, because it is unclear that such ground-truth is dominated by topology or attributes. RoadCA does not provide ground-truth. Baselines . As in Table 6 , we compared ASCENT over 13 13 baselines with 2 2 categories. First, NJW [ 5 ] , SCORE [ 6 ] , RSC [ 7 ] , SCORE+ [ 8 ] , ISC [ 9 ] , IBHCD [ 16 ] , and CDBH [ 29 ] are SC methods. Second, GraphEncoder ( GE ) [ 35 ] , SDCN [ 46 ] , MinCutPool ( MCP ) [ 44 ] , DMoN [ 45 ] , S3GC [ 38 ] , and MAGI [ 39 ] are DGC approaches. In particular, RSC , SCORE+ , ISC , IBHCD , and CDBH are DCSC baselines, where IBHCD and CDBH follow a new SC framework of iteratively searching each leading eigenvalue of the Bethe-Hessian matrix instead of that shown in Table 1 . Note that we consider graph clustering without attributes, while most of the second type of baselines were originally designed for attributed graphs. We tried widely-used strategies of (i) SVD on the adjacency matrix and (ii) one-hot encoding of degrees to derive feature inputs for them, with the best quality metrics reported. Evaluation Metrics . For datasets with feasible ground-truth, we used normalized mutual information ( NMI ) and accuracy ( AC ) as quality metrics. We also used the average conductance defined in ( 1 ) as an unsupervised metric for all the datasets. For those without feasible ground-truth, we followed prior work [ 67 , 68 ] to set K ∈ { 2 , 8 , 32 } K\in\{2,8,32\} and recorded the corresponding average conductance values. Usually, smaller conductance as well as larger NMI and AC indicate better clustering quality . We define that a method encounter the out-of-time exception if it fails to derive a feasible result within 10 4 10^{4} seconds. Hyper-parameters of all the methods were tuned based on the unsupervised average conductance metric. sections.heading: 6.2 Quality Evaluation
sections.text: For each setting of LFR-net, we independently generated 100 100 graphs and recorded the mean of all quality metrics over them. On each real dataset, we repeated the evaluation procedure over 5 5 random seeds and recorded the mean of each metric. Average results on synthetic and real graphs are depicted in Tables 7 and 8 , where a metric is in bold or underlined if it performs the best or second-best; OOM and OOT denote the out-of-memory and out-of-time exceptions. In most cases, SC methods have much better quality than DGC baselines. It indicates that some GNN-based approaches, with standard strategies to extract auxiliary features from topology, may fail to handle the high degree heterogeneity and weak clustering structures, although some of them are claimed to be effective for attributed graphs. Some DGC approaches also encounter the out-of-memory exception on large-scale graphs (e.g., Orkut ), due to the reconstruction of an N × N N\times N matrix (e.g., normalized adjacency matrices in GraphEncoder ) or space-consuming training procedures. In contrast, SC methods can derive feasible clustering results on all the datasets. Compared with SC algorithms using the standard procedures about graph Laplacian (i.e., ASCENT and those summarized in Table 1 ), IBHCD and CDBH that follow a new SC framework may easily suffer from low efficiency and cannot even derive feasible clustering results within 10 4 10^{4} seconds (i.e., out-of-time exception), especially for large N N s and K K s. ASCENT performs the best in most cases and can achieve significantly better quality than other DCSC baselines (e.g., with improvements from about 1 % 1\% to 40 % 40\% ) in some cases. It validates that ASCENT, a simple yet effective extension of DCSC, is more powerful in handling the high degree heterogeneity and weak clustering structures. sections.heading: 6.3 Efficiency Analysis
sections.text: We further evaluated the efficiency of each method in terms of its overall runtime (sec) to get a feasible clustering result. In particular, we recorded the time of different steps for each method. Results of the efficiency analysis on real datasets are depicted in Table 9 , where (i) ‘ τ \tau ’, (ii) ‘ED’, (iii) ‘C’, (iv) ‘T’, and (v) ‘I’ denote the time of (i) deriving node-wise corrections { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} (only for ASCENT), (ii) ED of graph Laplacian, (iii) K K Means clustering, (iv) training of a DGC method, and (v) inference of a DGC baseline. Compared with DGC approaches (e.g., GraphEncoder , S3GC , and MAGI ), which involve a time-consuming learning procedure (e.g., gradient descent to iteratively update model parameters), all the SC methods except IBHCD and CDBH can achieve significantly better efficiency in most cases. In particular, the overall runtime of IBHCD and CDBH may even be longer than those of DGC baselines, indicting their limitations of low efficiency. ED is the major bottleneck of most SC algorithms. For ASCENT, the derivation of node-wise corrections { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} would not significantly increase the overall runtime compared with other SC baselines. Surprisingly, ASCENT can even achieve better overall efficiency than some DCSC baselines (e.g., ISC on ogbn-Protein , RoadCA , and LiveJournal ), due to its faster ED. In summary, ASCENT can still ensure high efficiency close to that of conventional SC methods and much better than that of DGC approaches. sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we presented a condition-free analysis of DCSC from a pure spectral view. Different from prior studies based on random graph models (e.g., DCSBM), our analysis gives an upper bound for the number of mis-clustered nodes w.r.t. the optimal solution to average conductance minimization, without relying on additional conditions and random graph models. Our analysis also includes quantities that reveal impacts of (i) degree heterogeneity and (ii) weakness of clustering structures to the clustering quality of DCSC. Inspired by GNNs and their over-smoothing effect, we proposed ASCENT, a simple yet effective extension of DCSC. It follows a node-wise correction scheme that can assign nodes { v i } \{v_{i}\} with different corrections { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} via the GNN mean aggregation. In particular, ASCENT reduces to conventional DCSC methods when encountering over-smoothing. Some early stages before over-smoothing can potentially result in better clustering quality for ASCENT. We conclude this paper by discussing limitations of this paper and future research directions. Clustering on Attributed Graphs . As described in Section 3 , we followed the conventional problem statement of SC, where topology is the only available information source (i.e., without attributes), due to the complicated corrections between graph topology and attributes. In our future work, we will analyze DCSC on attributed graphs with the consideration of the possible inconsistency between the two sources [ 70 , 47 , 48 , 49 ] . Learnable Node-wise Corrections { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} . In ASCENT, we still set the node-wise corrections { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} by manually adjusting hyper-parameters { θ , L } \{\theta,L\} . We plan to extend it to a more advanced setting with learnable node-wise corrections { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} and provide theoretical analysis combined with recent advances in spectral-based GNNs [ 71 , 72 , 73 , 74 , 75 ] . Other Graph Clustering Objectives . In this study, we only considered the average conductance minimization objective (or equivalently normalized cut minimization) as defined in Definition 3.1 . SC can be considered as an approximated algorithm for a relaxed version of this objective. Some graph clustering algorithms may consider other objectives (e.g., ratio-cut minimization [ 21 ] and modularity maximization [ 40 , 76 , 77 ] ) that have relations close to average conductance minimization. We also plan to further extend our analysis to these objectives.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC Zero arXiv:2607.21435v1 [cs.SI] 23 Jul 2026 Revisiting Degree-Corrected Spectral Clustering: a Condition-Free Spectral Analysis and Extension Wei Li Xiaojian Li Meng Qin mengqin_az@foxmail.com Chaorui Zhang Weixi Zhang Yiwen Zhong Jianfeng Hou organization=School of Computer & Information Science, Fujian Agriculture & Forestry University, city=Fuzhou, state=Fujian, country=China organization=School of Mathematics & Statistics, Fuzhou University, city=Fuzhou, state=Fujian, country=China organization=Department of Strategic & Advanced Interdisciplinary Research, Pengcheng Laboratory (PCL), city=Shenzhen, state=Guangdong, country=China organization=Theory Lab, 2012 Labs, Huawei, state=Hong Kong SAR, country=China Abstract Spectral clustering is a representative graph clustering technique with strong interpretability and theoretical guarantees. Degree-corrected spectral clustering (DCSC) has emerged as the state-of-the-art for this technique. While prior studies have provided impressive theoretical insights for DCSC, their analyses typically depend on specific probabilistic frameworks (e.g., stochastic block models) and conditions. In this study, we explore an alternative condition-free analysis for the clustering quality of DCSC from a pure spectral view, without any random graph models. It gives bounds for the number of mis-clustered nodes w.r.t. the optimal partition of conductance minimization while involving quantities that indicate impacts of (i) degree heterogeneity and (ii) weakness of clustering structures to the clustering quality. Inspired by graph neural networks (GNNs) and their over-smoothing effect, we propose ASCENT (Adaptive Spectral ClustEring with Node-wise correcTion), a simple yet effective extension of DCSC. Different from most DCSC methods with a constant degree correction, ASCENT follows a node-wise correction scheme. It can assign different corrections for nodes via a GNN mean aggregator. We demonstrate that (i) ASCENT reduces to conventional DCSC methods when encountering over-smoothing; (ii) some early stages before over-smoothing can potentially result in better clustering quality. keywords graph clustering ,community detection ,degree-corrected spectral clustering ,spectral graph theory † † titlenote: This research was supported by the Interdisciplinary Frontier Research Project of PCL (2025QYB015), the National Key RD Program of China (2023YFA1010202), the Central Guidance on Local Science and Technology Development Fund of Fujian Province (2023L3003), the National Natural Science Foundation of China (11901094). † † corresponding: Corresponding author 1 Introduction Graph clustering (a.k.a. disjoint community detection) is a classic inference task that partitions nodes of a graph into densely connected groups (i.e., clusters or communities). Since the extracted clusters have been validated to correspond to some substructures of real-world systems (e.g., functional groups in protein interactions [ 1 ] ), many network applications are formulated as graph clustering, including protein complex detection [ 2 ] , cellular network decomposition [ 3 ] , and Internet traffic profiling [ 4 ] . Spectral clustering (SC) is one of the representative techniques for this task. As summarized in Table 1 , a typical SC algorithm includes the (I) eigen-decomposition (ED) on graph Laplacian, (II) arrangement of spectral embeddings, (III) normalization of embeddings, and (IV) K K Means clustering. In Table 1 , 𝐀 {\bf{A}} and 𝐃 {\bf{D}} are the adjacency matrix and degree diagonal matrix of a graph; K K is a pre-set number of clusters; λ r \lambda_{r} denotes the r r -th largest eigenvalue of graph Laplacian 𝐋 {\bf{L}} (e.g., 𝐋 := 𝐃 − 1 / 2 𝐀𝐃 − 1 / 2 {\bf{L}}:={\bf{D}}^{-1/2}{\bf{A}}{\bf{D}}^{-1/2} and 𝐋 := 𝐀 {\bf{L}}:={\bf{A}} for NJW [ 5 ] and SCORE [ 6 ] ) with 𝐮 r ∈ ℝ N {\bf{u}}_{r}\in\mathbb{R}^{N} as the corresponding eigenvector. Different SC algorithms usually differ in terms of the four steps. For instance, NJW , SCORE , and RSC [ 7 ] only consider eigenvectors ( 𝐮 1 , ⋯ , 𝐮 K ) ({\bf{u}}_{1},\cdots,{\bf{u}}_{K}) w.r.t. the leading K K eigenvalues. Step (II) of SCORE+ [ 8 ] and ISC [ 9 ] involves ( 𝐮 1 , ⋯ , 𝐮 K , 𝐮 K + 1 ) ({\bf{u}}_{1},\cdots,{\bf{u}}_{K},{\bf{u}}_{K+1}) , which are further reweighted by corresponding ( K + 1 ) (K+1) eigenvalues ( λ 1 , ⋯ , λ K , λ K + 1 ) (\lambda_{1},\cdots,\lambda_{K},\lambda_{K+1}) . NJW , RSC , and ISC adopt the row-wise l 2 l_{2} -normalization in step (III). SCORE and SCORE+ use (reweighted) 𝐮 1 {\bf{u}}_{1} to conduct column-wise normalization. Degree-corrected spectral clustering (DCSC), which is also defined as regularized spectral clustering in some literature [ 7 , 10 ] , has emerged as a state-of-the-art class of SC methods, due to its effectiveness in handling the high degree heterogeneity. Present Analysis & Extension . SC is a typical approximated algorithm for the NP-hard combinatorial optimization of graph-cut minimization [ 21 ] . From this perspective, some prior work [ 22 , 23 , 24 ] analyzed vanilla SC (e.g., NJW ) using the spectral graph theory. Motivated by these studies, we consider an alternative condition-free analysis for the clustering quality of DCSC from a pure spectral view instead of using any random graph models . Different from existing analyses with bounds related to random graph models (e.g., DCSBM in Table 2 ), we provide bounds for the number of mis-clustered nodes w.r.t. the optimal solution to average conductance minimization. In contrast to early spectral-based studies on vanilla SC [ 22 , 23 ] , our analysis also involves quantities about (i) degree heterogeneity and (ii) weakness of clustering structures, which can reveal impacts of these two aspects to the clustering quality of DCSC. Inspired by graph neural networks (GNNs), we propose ASCENT ( A daptive S pectral C lust E ring with N ode-wise correc T ion), a simple yet effective extension of DCSC. Instead of using a constant correction τ \tau for all nodes (e.g., RSC , SCORE+ , and ISC in Table 1 ), ASCENT adopts a node-wise correction scheme, where nodes { v i } \{v_{i}\} can be assigned with different corrections { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} . This scheme iteratively updates { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} via a GNN mean aggregator, where nodes { v i } \{v_{i}\} with more common neighbors (e.g., in the same cluster) are more likely to have closer { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} . Consistent with the over-smoothing effect of GNNs, { τ i } \{\tau_{i}\} finally converge to a constant. In this case, ASCENT reduces to conventional DCSC methods. Our experiments demonstrate that some early stages of this updating procedure (i.e., before over-smoothing) can potentially result in better clustering quality. We also extend our analysis to a unified framework that provides bounds for a series of SC methods. Based on this framework, we try to answer the following three questions. • Q1 : Can DCSC achieve a tighter bound than vanilla SC? • Q2 : Can ISC achieve a tighter bound than RSC ? • Q3 : Can ASCENT achieve a tighter bound than ISC ? Answering Q1 - Q3 may help interpret why a DCSC method outperforms others. Whereas, most related studies tend to focus on a single algorithm and may not be able to answer these questions explored in this paper. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. [ 33 ] and Su et al. [ 34 ] . GraphEncoder [ 35 ] and DNR [ 36 ] are early studies that learn low-dimensional community-preserving representations (or embeddings) by reconstructing topology-related features (e.g., normalized adjacency matrices and modularity matrices) via a deep auto-encoder. THESAURUS [ 37 ] enhances the ability of learned embeddings to capture implicit graph clustering structures by using (i) context-aware semantic prototypes, (ii) a cross-view assignment prediction objective, and (iii) Gromov-Wasserstein Optimal Transport. For clustering on large-scale graphs, Devvrit et al. [ 38 ] proposed S3GC , which learns scalable community-preserving embeddings via GNN-based contrastive learning. MAGI [ 39 ] extends S3GC to incorporate the modularity maximization objective [ 40 ] from the view of contrastive learning. A downstream clustering algorithm (e.g., K K Means) is usually applied to the learned embeddings to derive a feasible clustering result for these approaches. DGCluster [ 41 ] also uses the modularity maximization objective to optimize GNN, which outputs community-preserving embeddings, but derives final clustering results using BIRCH [ 42 ] . ClusterNet [ 43 ] , MinCutPool [ 44 ] , and DMoN [ 45 ] adopt a deep end-to-end structure, which contains a GNN and an output module (e.g., a multi-layer perceptron for deriving clustering results), to fit classic graph clustering objectives (e.g., graph-cut minimization and modularity maximization). SDCN [ 46 ] combines the deep auto-encoder with GNN and uses a dual self-supervised mechanism to unify these two deep architectures. Most of the aforementioned methods, especially those based on GNNs, were originally designed for attributed graphs and may not fully consider the complicated correlations between graph topology and attributes (see Section 3 for further discussions). Our empirical experiments (see Section 6 ) demonstrated that when attributes are unavailable, these state-of-the-art DGC methods may not outperform SC approaches.
